angle: you are Phil Katz with a court deadline; the fix is LZ-style pointers (go back 13, copy 5); ZIP released two weeks after the deadline
title: He got sued, so he invented the ZIP file
description:
In 1988 Phil Katz was sued by SEA, the makers of ARC, over his much faster compatible program, PKARC. The settlement said he had to stop shipping ARC-compatible software after January 31, 1989. Two weeks later, on February 14, 1989, he released a new format into the public domain: ZIP.

The core idea behind ZIP compression: never store anything twice. When text repeats, store a short note instead, like "go back 13, copy 5" for the second TO BE in TO BE OR NOT TO BE. English text usually shrinks to about a third (checked with the Deflate method used in .zip files on five English documents: 32 to 35%). Sources: Wikipedia, Phil Katz / ARC (file format) / ZIP (file format).
facts_checked: SEA sued Katz for trademark and copyright infringement; settlement announced August 2, 1988; PKWARE could not distribute ARC-compatible programs after January 31, 1989 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Katz, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARC_(file_format))
ZIP released into the public domain February 14, 1989; spec APPNOTE.TXT; Katz declared it free for competing software (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZIP_(file_format), Phil_Katz)
ARC 'quickly dropped out of common use'; ZIP became the standard (ARC_(file_format))
Windows: Plus! 98 add-on, native 'Compressed Folders' from Windows Me (2000) (ZIP_(file_format))
Deflate (LZ77 + Huffman) is the standard ZIP method since PKZIP 2.0 (1993) (ZIP_(file_format))
TO BE OR NOT TO BE: second TO BE at index 13, back 13 copy 5 (verify.py, LZ77 round trip)
English text with zlib/Deflate: 32-35% of original size on 5 documents (verify.py)
banana = B, A, N, back 2 copy 3 (verify.py; answer not given in video)

beats.say: You're a programmer in 1988, and you're being sued over your own app.
It shrinks files, much faster than theirs. But the deal you sign says: stop shipping it by January 31st, 1989. You need a brand new way to make files smaller.
Here's the trick. Files repeat themselves. Look at this line.
To be or not to be. The second to be is an exact copy.
So don't store it twice. Store a tiny note instead: go back 13, copy 5.
That's your way out. Real files are full of repeats. Spaces, common words, whole lines of code. A page of English shrinks to about a third.
Two weeks after the deadline, on Valentine's Day 1989, you release it. You call it zip.
You give the format away for free, so anyone can use it. The old one fades out, and by 2000 Windows opens zips on its own.
Every zip you've opened still runs on that idea: never store anything twice. So how would you shrink the word banana? Tell me below.
